newsitem.title: USA: Bird-like dinosaur reported found in Patagonia. [CORRECTED 21:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bird-like dinosaur reported found in Patagonia. [CORRECTED 21:40 GMT]

text.p: An Argentinian (corrects nationality from Peruvian) researcher on Tuesday reported finding bones of the most bird-like dinosaur ever discovered, an ostrich-sized, meat-eater that ran around flapping wing-like forearms to keep its balance.

The discovery helps explain how the forearms of some dinosaurs evolved into wings that power today's birds, believed by many paleontologists to be direct descendants of dinosaurs, said Fernando Novas who made the find in a remote area of Patagonia.

"Birds are living dinosaurs," Novas told a news conference at the National Geographic Society which funded his field work. He said he was "astonished" on examining bones he found in the sandstone sediment of a river that once flowed into the Pacific Ocean to realise they were similar to those of the world's oldest known bird.
But this creature, he said, while it is "the most bird-like dinosaur ever discovered," is not an ancestor of today's birds but an evolutionary dead-end for this particular species.
Novas said he made that deduction because the oldest known bird evolved about 145 million years ago, while the newly discovered dinosaur lived 90 million years ago.
The creature was named unenlagia comahuensis, based on the words for "half bird from northwest Patagonia" in the language of the region's Mapuche Indians.

Novas, who works at the Museo Argentino de Ciencias Naturales in Buenos Aires, said the animal was nearly four feet (1.2 meters) tall at the hip and about seven and one-half feet (2.3 meters) long. Its structure was similar to an ostrich, he said, and its shape may have resembled Velociraptors, the creatures that sped across the screen in the movie "Jurassic Park."

In an article in Nature magazine where Novas published his findings, he said the creature could use its forerarms to grasp prey "and probably also in maintainance of balance and to control its body attitude while running and leaping."

It was not known if the wing-like forearm was feathered, he said, but if it was it would have provided "an airfoil, a new control surface" for balance and manoeuvrability, much the way man uses his arms for balance while skating or surfing.

The dinosaur had a shoulder joint socket that faced to the side, as does a bird's. It could flap its arms in an "upstroke" needed for flight, though it did not fly, and could fold its arms as a bird does so that the upper bones lay close to its body.
"I was searching for dinosaurs," Novas told reporters. "I never thought to find such beautiful treasures."
